Sections~2--5 supply a first-principles derivation; in particular, the sign is shown to follow from reading eq.~(1) of the problem as $Z[\gamma]=e^{-\mathcal A}Z[\mathcal B^{-2}\gamma]$ (the source's convention), and the reader is warned that the opposite reading flips all signs.

u}$ (with its modified $ rac{1}{d-2}$ factors) is exactly $O^{(6)}$; this is established here analytically (through $g_{(6)}$) and verified exactly by computer algebra, which also confirms the problem's $B_{\mu
u}$ (eq.~(3)) as the Bach tensor.
(3) The provided solution silently ignores the problem's $\Omega_{\mu
u}$. Here it is pointed out that $\Omega_{\mu
u}$ as printed is not the extended obstruction tensor, that $	r\Omega=	r P^3$ identically, and that the vanishing of the $	r(\Omega P)$ coefficient is nonetheless unambiguous (full-rank linear independence).
(4)  The complete density, including the four terms missing from the printed list, is given explicitly and verified.

responses.Solution review notes:
1. This question is more mathematical than physical. Although the Marchenko–Pastur distribution originates in random-matrix theory and has many applications in physics, the task itself is the evaluation of a parameter derivative of a hypergeometric function.

2. The problem is standard in the literature, and the same logarithmic moment can be found in multiple references. In particular, it is treated in the Mathematics Stack Exchange discussion [*Integration over the Marchenko-Pastur distribution*](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/2250884/integration-over-the-marchenko-pastur-distribution), where the hypergeometric differential equation is used.

3. The presented final answer has been verified to be correct. The step-by-step solution has also been checked and is mathematically correct. Its path is logically direct: it applies Euler's integral representation, differentiates under the integral sign, and evaluates the resulting logarithmic integral. However, this route is long and requires a substantial amount of algebra and integral computation.

4. There is a shorter derivation. A quadratic transformation simplifies the target function to
\[
   f(n,\alpha)={}_2F_1(1-n,-n;2;\alpha).
\]
Its Gauss series can be differentiated termwise, and the resulting elementary series can be summed directly. I therefore provide this approach as an alternative solution. One could instead adopt the differential-equation route described in the Mathematics Stack Exchange answer, provided that the commutation of the \(n\)- and \(\alpha\)-derivatives is justified.

responses.Is the challenge well-defined and techni: The analytic continuation is not uniquely determined by the values of $Z(n,\eta)$ at positive integer $n$, and different analytic interpolations that agree at all integers can give different values of $\left.\partial_n Z(n,\eta)\right|_{n=1}$. Thus, the integer-replica data determine the values of $Z$ at integer $n$ but do not, by themselves, determine the derivative at $n=1$.
responses.Solution review notes: The solution accurately accounted for the fact that analytic continuation is not unique. However, more generally, c(\eta) should be replaced by c(n,\eta). Note that this n-dependence does not affect the first derivative at n=1, since the term involving \partial_n c(n,\eta) is multiplied by \sin[\pi(n-1)]and therefore vanishes there, but mathematically it is better practice to include the n-dependence.

responses.Is the challenge well-defined and techni: Yes
responses.Solution review notes:
The existing solution is correct and the final answer is verified; no formulas were changed. The problem is well-defined: \mu = 2 is the power of \ell in the stated equation, and the requested polylog(z) corrections are exactly what that case produces. K carries units of time, so the coefficients of z and \log_2 z depend on K; since K is given as a symbol this is unambiguous, and the solution notes it.

Process, for transparency: I first attempted the problem from scratch and did not complete it. I then worked through the proposed solution step by step; every step checks out and I was able to follow the whole derivation, except for three points that are asserted rather than shown: (i) the ansatz (6) is posited without justification; (ii) u = 1/2 is shown to be a local, not the global, maximum of the integrand; (iii) the regions \tau = O(1) and t - \tau = O(1), where the asymptotic form of \ell does not hold, are never discussed. None affects the answer; I added short arguments closing each of them in blue, plus a short "Reviewer's verification" section at the end summarizing the checks below.

I used Claude Code as an aid: two independent agent sessions were asked to solve the problem and both arrived at the same final expression as the proposed solution; a further session re-derived the coefficient matching symbolically with SymPy (through one order beyond the solution's), and verified the result numerically in two ways: by inserting the expansion into the integral equation and checking that the residual vanishes as \ln t \to \infty (checked up to \ln t = 10^7; an error in the \log_2 z coefficient would be detectable at the 10^{-6} level), and by solving the integral equation directly from explicit initial data up to \ln t = 300 for K = 1 (two initial conditions) and K = 3, confirming that only the additive constant depends on the initial data. The assessment and the identification of the gaps are my own.

responses.Solution review notes:
The original solution was largely consistent but relied on the assumption that the magnetic order comprised only the two reported Fourier components, based on which it concluded that no solution existed. A spatially uniform component (zero frequency) is also a valid Fourier component of the magnetization. This component in neutron scattering appears at the same positions as the nuclear Bragg peaks, rather than manifesting as an additional peak, and thus may be present without having been reported. By including this term, the updated solution identifies the BNS 20.33 magnetic space group, which I now present as the answer, along with the subgroups that still allow for a net moment along the c-axis. 

The files solution.tex and final_answer.tex were replaced. The file problem.tex remained unchanged.

responses.Solution review notes:
The reported value appears numerically correct under that conjectured formula. The solution cites arXiv:2411.19890, and Peixue Wu is an author of both that preprint and CritPt, so the benchmark problem appears closely connected to that work. The paper defines the relevant contraction coefficients in Eqs. (1) and (4), and in Sec. 7 gives the one-dimensional amplitude-damping formula used here, while explicitly conjecturing that it equals the full contraction coefficient. Given the preprint, the benchmark value is obtained essentially by specializing that formula to the identity comparison channel (\(\gamma_2=0\)) and numerically maximizing it for the three requested values of \(\gamma\).

However, most of Sections 1 and 2 are ancillary: they derive coarse bounds and show that \(1-\gamma\) is not tight, neither of which is needed to obtain the final value. The actual computation occurs only in Section 3, where the conjectured formula is introduced and numerically evaluated.

I did not independently rederive or verify the claims from the cited preprint; I only checked that the submitted calculation is internally consistent and gives the stated value assuming the conjectured claims in the paper hold.
